aspects.fertilizer:
General Information:
Seasonal maize sowing is the entire month of July, changed from July 20 to August 20. Increased heat requires higher fertilizer and water doses. Sow seed 1.5 to 2 inches deep and keep fields weed-free for the first 50 days. Apply 3 to 4 trolley per acre well-rotted farmyard manure 1 month before sowing. Apply sowing fertilizers before making ridges. Apply all potash at sowing because maize absorbs 70 to 80 percent of its potash by flowering. Sweet corn and popcorn use the same fertilizer rates as general varieties. Apply zinc sulphate at 10 kg per acre or 6 kg per acre. Apply borax 11 percent boron at 3 kg per acre.

Hybrid Varieties - Poor Soil:
For soil with organic matter under 0.87 percent, phosphorus under 7 ppm, and potash under 80 ppm, apply 119 kg nitrogen, 69 kg phosphorus, and 50 kg potash per acre. At sowing, apply 3 bags DAP, 2 bags SOP, and 0.25 bag urea, or 7.5 bags single super phosphate, 2 bags SOP, and 1.5 bags urea. At 5 to 6 leaves, apply 1.25 bags urea. At 8 to 10 leaves, apply 1.25 bags urea. Apply 1.25 bags urea 1 week before flowering.

Hybrid Varieties - Medium Soil:
For soil with organic matter 0.87 to 1.29 percent, phosphorus 7 to 14 ppm, and potash 80 to 180 ppm, apply 92 kg nitrogen, 58 kg phosphorus, and 37 kg potash per acre. At sowing, apply 1.5 bags DAP and 1.5 bags SOP, or 6.5 bags single super phosphate, 1.5 bags SOP, and 1 bag urea. At 5 to 6 leaves, apply 1 bag urea. At 8 to 10 leaves, apply 1 bag urea. Apply 1 bag urea 1 week before flowering.

Hybrid Varieties - Fertile Soil:
For soil with organic matter above 1.29 percent, phosphorus above 14 ppm, and potash above 180 ppm, apply 75 kg nitrogen, 46 kg phosphorus, and 25 kg potash per acre. At sowing, apply 2 bags DAP and 1 bag SOP, or 5 bags single super phosphate, 1 bag SOP, and 0.75 bag urea. At 5 to 6 leaves, apply 1 bag urea. At 8 to 10 leaves, apply 0.75 bag urea. Apply 0.75 bag urea 1 week before flowering.

Irrigated General Varieties:
Poor soil with organic matter under 0., phosphorus under 7 ppm, and potash under 80 ppm requires 92 kg nitrogen, 58 kg phosphorus, and 37 kg potash per acre. Medium soil with organic matter 0. to 1., phosphorus 7 to 14 ppm, and potash 80 to 180 ppm requires 80 kg nitrogen, 46 kg phosphorus, and 37 kg potash per acre. Fertile soil with organic matter over 1., phosphorus over 14 ppm, and potash over 180 ppm requires 70 kg nitrogen, 35 kg phosphorus, and 25 kg potash per acre.

Rain-fed General Varieties:
Apply all fertilizer at sowing. Fertile soil with organic matter over 1.29 percent, phosphorus over 14 ppm, and potash over 180 ppm requires 70 kg nitrogen, 35 kg phosphorus, and 25 kg potash per acre. Low rainfall areas require 34 kg nitrogen, 23 kg phosphorus, and 12 kg potash per acre. Per-acre options are 1 bag DAP, 2 bags ammonium nitrate, and 0.5 bag SOP; or 1 bag DAP, 1 bag urea, and 0.5 bag SOP; or 2.5 bags single super phosphate, 1.5 bags urea, and 0.5 bag SOP. High rainfall areas require 46 kg nitrogen, 34 kg phosphorus, and 25 kg potash per acre. Per-acre options are 1.5 bags DAP, 2.5 bags ammonium nitrate, and 1 bag SOP; or 1.5 bags DAP, 1.5 bags urea, and 1 bag SOP; or 4 bags single super phosphate, 2 bags urea, and 1 bag SOP.

Deficiencies and Disease Management:
Nitrogen deficiency stunts growth and yellows leaves in a V shape from tips before browning. Phosphorus deficiency halts growth, weakens roots, and turns leaf tips purple. Potash deficiency produces white spots on leaf edges that turn brown. To control stem and cob rot, plant resistant varieties, use balanced fertilizer, and destroy residues. For stem rot, avoid potash deficiency, avoid excess nitrogen, avoid planting maize in affected fields for years, rotate crops, treat seeds with fungicide, and drain rain promptly.
aspects.harvesting:
Punjab:
Maize processing factories operate in various areas of Punjab. Maize is used to make starch, edible oil, glucose, custard, jelly, cornflakes, and popcorn.

Harvest Dates:
Maize harvesting takes place between 15 May and 15 June, and between 15 October and 15 November.

Harvest Indicators:
Harvest when inner husks dry, grains turn shiny and hard, fingernails cannot pierce grains, and a black layer forms at the pointed tip of grains. Grain moisture at this stage is approximately 30 to 35 percent. Harvesting prematurely causes incomplete grain filling, reduces yield, and harms seed germination. Delaying harvest leads to lodging and bird damage. Rainfall on lodged crops promotes fungal growth and toxic aflatoxin production.

Drying and Shelling:
Separate cobs from plants and husks. Dry cobs rapidly on purpose-built paved platforms, never on unpaved ground or bare soil. Turn cobs continuously every day for uniform drying. Cover cobs with tarpaulins if rain is expected, and remove tarpaulins after rainfall. Grain is sufficiently dry when striking cobs together detaches grains and biting a grain produces a cracking sound. Moisture is approximately 15 percent at this stage. Use a sheller to separate grains from cobs.

Storage and Fumigation:
Clean the warehouse thoroughly before storage. Spray recommended pesticide and seal doors and windows for 4 hours to eliminate insects. Maize can be stored as whole cobs or grains. Ensure grain moisture is below 10 percent before storage. Clean grains to remove broken seeds, straw, and dirt. Keep newly harvested stock separate from older stock. Label stored maize according to its intended use. Apply 30 to 35 tablets of aluminum phosphide per 1000 cubic feet of storage volume, especially during the monsoon season. Keep the store closed for at least one week following fumigation. Use hermetic bags or hermetic cocoons for long-term storage without fumigation.

Aflatoxin Prevention:
Harvest maize when grain moisture is 30 percent or lower. Dry cobs quickly on paved floors. Protect the produce from rain and moisture at every post-harvest stage. Store maize at moisture levels below 10 percent.

Disease Management:
Sow varieties resistant to stem rot and cob rot. Avoid weak-stemmed and lodging-prone varieties. Treat seeds with recommended fungicide. Maintain balanced fertilization, prevent potash deficiency, and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer. Do not plant maize in stem-rot-affected fields for several years and follow crop rotation. Uproot and destroy infected plants with their roots at any growth stage. Maintain recommended plant-to-plant and ridge distances. Irrigate as needed and drain excess rainwater immediately. Control cob-boring pests with insecticides. Destroy all crop residues immediately after harvest.
aspects.irrigation:
**General Maize Sowing:**
Seasonal maize was previously sown from July 20 to August 20.
In recent years, the recommended sowing time for seasonal maize is the entire month of July.
Apply higher quantities of fertilizers and water to withstand increased heat intensity.

**Southern Punjab Kharif Maize:**
Sow Kharif maize after July 25.

**Spring Maize:**
Spring maize generally requires 12 to 14 irrigations.
Cultivate varieties resistant to high temperatures.

**Kharif Maize:**
Kharif maize generally requires 10 to 12 irrigations.

**Irrigation Management:**
For flat fields, apply the first irrigation 10 to 12 days after emergence.
For ridge and bed sowing, apply light irrigations as needed to maintain wattar moisture until emergence.
Shorten the irrigation interval during severe heat.
Increase the irrigation interval when temperatures decrease.
Irrigate according to crop requirements to reduce the impact of unexpected heatwaves during pollination.
Do not allow water stress from flowering until grain formation, especially during flowering, pollination, and the milky stage.
Check the weather forecast before applying irrigation.
Immediately drain excess water from the field after heavy rainfall.
Follow irrigation methods specified in the booklet.

**Waxy Maize:**
Apply an irrigation on the fourth day after sowing to facilitate germination and emergence.

**Stem Rot Management:**
Sow varieties resistant to stem rot.
Treat seeds with recommended fungicide before planting.
Maintain balanced field fertility and prevent potash deficiency in the soil.
Do not apply excessive nitrogen fertilizer.
Maintain recommended spacing between plants and ridges.
Irrigate according to crop need and drain excess rainwater immediately.
Pull out and destroy affected plants along with roots at any growth stage.
Destroy crop residues as soon as possible after harvest.
Do not grow maize in affected fields for the next few years and rotate crops.

**Mite Management and Soil:**
Never cultivate maize on sandy soil.
Do not allow fields to dry out and keep them in wattar moisture condition.
Keep fields, water channels, and ridges free of weeds throughout the year.
Destroy crop stubble and rotavate empty land.
Apply spray in consultation with agricultural experts if an attack occurs.
aspects.machinery:
Land Preparation:
It is better to level the land with a laser land leveler before field preparation.
Run a rotavator first to break down stubble or soil clods left from the previous crop.
Plow and plank three to four times for good land preparation.
Use a deep plow if a hardpan layer is present in the soil.

Sowing:
An automatic maize planter is very useful for timely and effective maize sowing.
Sowing with a planter ensures better and uniform crop germination.
Using a planter saves labor and reduces cultivation costs.

Post-Harvest Handling and Drying:
Separate cobs from the plants and spread them on platforms built for this purpose.
Turn the cobs continuously every day until they dry uniformly.
Cover cobs with a tarpaulin if rain is expected, and remove the tarpaulin after the rain passes.
Maize is well dried when hitting cobs against each other detaches grains, and a grain breaks with a snapping sound when bitten.
Grain moisture is approximately 15 percent at this stage.

Shelling:
Use a sheller to separate grains from the cobs when grain moisture reaches approximately 15 percent.

Storage:
Moisture in the grains must be less than 10 percent if the produce is to be stored.
aspects.other:
**Crop Rotations:**
One-year crop rotations include Kharif maize followed by wheat.
One-year crop rotations include potato followed by spring maize.
One-year crop rotations include Kharif maize followed by berseem.
One-year crop rotations include coarse rice varieties followed by potato followed by spring maize.
Two-year crop rotations include Kharif maize followed by wheat, then Kharif maize followed by berseem.
Two-year crop rotations include Kharif maize followed by wheat, then cotton followed by berseem.

**Soil Selection:**
Select heavy loam and deep fertile soil for maize cultivation.
Soil must have good organic matter content and strong water absorption capacity.

**Land Preparation:**
Plough and plank three to four times for proper land preparation.
Run a deep plough if a hardpan is present in the soil.
Use a laser land leveler to make the field evenly flat.

**Climate Impact and Heat Management:**
Severe heat during the pollination stage in spring maize causes severe negative effects on the crop.
Irrigate according to crop water needs to reduce the impact of an unexpected heatwave during pollination.
Follow recommended production technology.
Stay updated with weather forecasts.

**Government and Planning:**
The provincial government sets the maize cultivated area target for each district with federal government approval.
The Deputy Director of Agriculture Extension prepares an integrated strategy to increase maize production in the district.
The Deputy Director of Agriculture Extension informs the district and provincial administrations about this strategy.
The Deputy Director of Agriculture Extension mobilizes all extension staff to achieve the assigned targets.
aspects.overview:
**General Overview:**
Maize is an important cash and kharif cereal crop grown for human food and livestock fodder.
Two crops are grown annually: spring and kharif.
Most maize production is used in poultry feed.
It is utilized for starch, edible oil, biofuel, livestock green fodder, silage, wanda feed, paper manufacturing, and glue.
Spring maize experiences lower temperatures in early growth followed by longer days and abundant sunlight, resulting in a longer growth duration and 25 to 30 percent higher per-acre yield than kharif maize.

**Soil Requirements:**
Loam, heavy loam, and deep fertile soils with good organic matter and strong water absorption capacity are suitable.
Sandy, waterlogged, and saline soils are not suitable.

**Punjab Recommended Synthetic Varieties:**
All recommended varieties are suitable for both spring and kharif seasons.
Malka-2016 has yellow grain and yields 86 maunds.
Gohar-19 has white grain and yields 81 maunds.
Sahiwal Gold has yellow grain and yields 91 maunds.
CIMMYT Pak has white grain and yields 71 maunds.
Pop-1 popcorn was approved in 2019, has yellow grain, yields 55 maunds per acre, and matures in 100 to 105 days in spring and 90 to 95 days in kharif.
Sweet-1 sweet corn was approved in 2019, has yellow grain, yields 44 maunds per acre, and matures in 100 to 105 days in spring and 90 to 95 days in kharif.

**Spring Crop Statistics:**
In 2019-20, area was 1012.6 thousand acres (409.8 thousand hectares), production was 3907.5 thousand tons, and average yield was 9535 kg/ha (96.47 maunds/acre).
In 2020-21, area was 1146.0 thousand acres (463.8 thousand hectares), production was 4491.1 thousand tons, and average yield was 9684 kg/ha (97.97 maunds/acre).
In 2021-22, area was 1384.0 thousand acres (560.1 thousand hectares), production was 4307.7 thousand tons, and average yield was 7691 kg/ha (77.81 maunds/acre).
In 2022-23, area was 1620.0 thousand acres (655.6 thousand hectares), production was 6036.7 thousand tons, and average yield was 9208 kg/ha (93.16 maunds/acre).
In 2023-24, area was 1191.0 thousand acres (482.0 thousand hectares), production was 4172.9 thousand tons, and average yield was 8658 kg/ha (87.59 maunds/acre).

**Kharif Crop Statistics:**
In 2019-20, area was 1322.4 thousand acres (535.1 thousand hectares), production was 3087.2 thousand tons, and average yield was 5769 kg/ha (58.36 maunds/acre).
In 2020-21, area was 1198.1 thousand acres (484.8 thousand hectares), production was 3548.8 thousand tons, and average yield was 7319 kg/ha (74.05 maunds/acre).
In 2021-22, area was 1545.1 thousand acres (625.2 thousand hectares), production was 4321.1 thousand tons, and average yield was 6911 kg/ha (69.92 maunds/acre).
In 2022-23, area was 1452.6 thousand acres (587.8 thousand hectares), production was 4017.7 thousand tons, and average yield was 6835 kg/ha (69.15 maunds/acre).
In 2023-24, area was 1647.6 thousand acres (666.7 thousand hectares), production was 4603.0 thousand tons, and average yield was 6903 kg/ha (69.84 maunds/acre).

**Extension Activities:**
The first extension step is publishing the maize production plan detailing basic cultivation principles.
Agricultural experts will conduct district and tehsil level trainings for extension workers and farmers on modern maize production technology.
aspects.pests_diseases:
Northern Areas:
Smut from Ustilago maydis creates black powder galls. Plant resistant varieties and avoid maize for several years.

Rain-fed and Sandy Areas:
Termites damage roots and stems. Apply Fipronil 5SC at 1 liter per acre during rauni or broadcast Fipronil 80WG at 60 grams into soil during preparation. Avoid raw dung. Avoid sandy soil because mites cause 40 percent loss in hot dry weather.

Diseases:
Sow seed 1.5 to 2 inches deep. Keep weed-free for 50 days. Soil fungi wither seedlings at 3 to 9 inches. Stalk rot from Erwinia chrysanthemi, Macrophomina phaseolina, or Cephalosporium maydis rots the second node and shrivels grains. Maintain potash and drain rainwater. Helminthosporium turcicum and Helminthosporium maydis cause 6-inch blight spots. Diplodia maydis, Fusarium, Nigrospora oryzae, Penicillium, and Aspergillus cause cob rot.

Shoot Fly and Maize Borer:
Shoot fly larvae live 12 days and attack emerging spring and sweet maize for 20 to 30 days. Seed treatments giving 40 days protection per kilogram: Clothianidin + Azoxystrobin 62.5WS 9 g, Imidacloprid + Tebuconazole 37.25FS 10 ml, Thiamethoxam 70WS 3 g, Imidacloprid 70WS 5 g, or Thiamethoxam 350FS 10 ml. Spray Emamectin benzoate 1.9EC at 200 ml or Bifenthrin 10EC at 250 ml per acre at emergence and 8 to 10 days later.
For maize borer in seasonal or sweet maize, place 20 Trichogramma cards per acre every 10 to 15 days until pollen forms. Apply per acre into whorls: Chlorantraniliprole 0.4% G 4 kg, Fipronil 0.3% G 8 kg, Emamectin benzoate + Fipronil 0.35G 8 kg, or Chlorantraniliprole + Thiamethoxam 0.6% GR 4 kg.

Other Pests:
Spray per acre:
For jassid: Thiamethoxam 25WG 24 g, Carbosulfan 20EC 500 ml, or Imidacloprid 200SL 200 ml.
For aphids: Acetamiprid 20SP 125 g, Carbosulfan 20SC 250 ml, Imidacloprid 200SL 200 to 250 ml, or Acephate 97% DF 250 g.
For American bollworm: Spinetoram 120SC 100 ml, Chlorantraniliprole 20SC 50 ml, Flubendiamide 480SC 50 ml, or Spinosad 240SC 40 ml.
For armyworm: Chlorantraniliprole 20SC 50 ml, Indoxacarb 150SC 175 ml, Flubendiamide 480SC 50 ml, Emamectin 1.9EC 200 ml, Lufenuron 5% EC 200 ml, or Methoxyfenozide 120EC 200 ml.

Fall Armyworm:
Larvae grow 1.25 to 1.50 inches over 18 to 30 days and adults live 3 to 20 days. Larvae cause 30 to 35 percent loss on 30 to 40-day crops. Scout twice weekly and treat early instars in afternoons. Per acre sprays: Spinetoram 120SC 100 ml, Chlorantraniliprole 200SC 100 ml, Emamectin benzoate 1.9EC 240 ml, Lufenuron 5% EC 240 ml, Chlorantraniliprole + Emamectin benzoate 16% WDG 100 g, or Emamectin benzoate 1.9EC + Lufenuron 5% EC at 200+200 ml. Or whorl-apply 8 kg of Chlorantraniliprole + Emamectin benzoate 0.26% G or Fipronil + Emamectin benzoate 0.35G.

Storage:
Harvest at 30 percent or lower moisture and store below 10 percent moisture. Close sprayed stores 4 hours. Fumigate with 30 to 35 Aluminum phosphide tablets per 1000 cubic feet for at least one week.
aspects.sowing:
**Sowing Dates:**
Spring maize sowing is recommended from mid-January to 10 February, or late January to 28 February. March sowing faces severe heat during cob emergence which drops yields. Kharif maize sowing is recommended for the entire month of July, or 15 July to 15 August. South Punjab Kharif sowing should occur after 25 July. Kharif maize for green cobs can be sown until late August.

**Barani Punjab (Attock, Jhelum, Rawalpindi, Chakwal, Gujrat):**
Sow maize at monsoon onset using a drill, planter, or pora at 2.5 feet row spacing. Select early varieties based on follow-up crops. Thin the crop at 4 to 6 inches height by removing weak and diseased plants. Maintain plant spacing at 6 to 7 inches for early varieties and 7 to 8 inches for late varieties.

**Land Preparation and Planting:**
Plough deeply every 2 to 3 years to break hardpan. Level fields with a laser land leveler. Seed depth in loam and heavy loam soils must be 1.5 to 2 inches. Keep fields weed-free for the first 50 days. Ensure effective pest control and uniform fertilizer broadcasting. Never replant missing spots because gap-filled plants cannot match crop height and yield poorly. An automatic maize planter ensures uniform emergence and saves labor and costs.

**Irrigated Ridge Sowing:**
Make east-west ridges 2.25 to 2.5 feet apart. Dibble single seeds on ridge slopes slightly above the water level immediately after light watering. In spring, dibble on the southern side for full sunlight. In Kharif, dibble on the northern side. In spring, space hybrid varieties 6 inches and common varieties 7 to 8 inches. In Kharif, space hybrid varieties 7 inches and common varieties 8 to 9 inches.

**Irrigated Bed Sowing:**
Make beds 3, 3.5, or 4 feet apart with 2.5-foot tops, dibbling seeds on both sides. In spring, space hybrid varieties 8 to 9 inches and common varieties 10 to 11 inches. In Kharif, space hybrid varieties 10 inches and common varieties 11 to 12 inches.

**Plant Populations and Special Types:**
Sweet corn and popcorn require 8 inches plant spacing in spring and 9 inches in Kharif. Per-acre Kharif targets are 30,000 plants for hybrids and 23,000 to 26,000 for common varieties. On 2.25-foot ridges, per-acre plant counts are 38,720 at 6 inches, 33,189 at 7 inches, 29,040 at 8 inches, 25,813 at 9 inches, and 23,232 at 10 inches. On 2.5-foot ridges, counts are 34,848 at 6 inches, 29,870 at 7 inches, 26,136 at 8 inches, 23,232 at 9 inches, and 19,913 at 10 inches. On beds, counts at 8 inches spacing are 43,560 for 3-foot beds, 37,337 for 3.5-foot beds, and 32,670 for 4-foot beds. At 9 inches spacing, counts are 38,720 for 3-foot beds, 33,189 for 3.5-foot beds, and 29,040 for 4-foot beds.

**Heat and Irrigation Management:**
Sow heat-tolerant varieties in spring. Avoid water deficiency during pollination in heatwaves. Shorten irrigation intervals during extreme heat and drain excess rainwater. Apply higher fertilizer and water doses to withstand severe heat. Stay updated with weather forecasts.
aspects.varieties:
**General Varieties Punjab:**
Malka-2016 approved in 2016 has yellow grain, yields 86 maunds per acre, and matures in 115 days in spring and 100 days in Kharif.
Gohar-19 approved in 2019 has white grain, yields 81 maunds per acre, and matures in 105 to 110 days in spring and 95 to 100 days in Kharif.
Sahiwal Gold approved in 2019 has yellow grain, yields 91 maunds per acre, and matures in 110 to 115 days in spring and 100 to 105 days in Kharif.
Samit Pak approved in 2019 has white grain, yields 71 maunds per acre, and matures in 90 to 100 days in spring and 85 to 90 days in Kharif.
Pop-1 popcorn approved in 2019 has yellow grain, yields 55 maunds per acre, and matures in 100 to 105 days in spring and 90 to 95 days in Kharif.
Sweet-1 sweet corn has yellow grain and yields 44 maunds per acre.
All these varieties suit spring and Kharif seasons. General varieties are also suitable for green fodder.

**Barani Punjab:**
In Attock, Jhelum, Rawalpindi, Chakwal, and Gujrat, sow maize according to monsoon onset.
Sow early varieties based on earliness considering the following crop.
Malka-2016, Gohar-19, and Sahiwal Gold are best for rain-fed areas lacking adequate irrigation.

**Southern Punjab:**
Sow Kharif maize after July 25.

**Hybrid Maize:**
Hybrids give high yields, uniform growth, more cobs with thick heavy grains, and lodging resistance.
Research Institute Yousafwala District Sahiwal developed hybrids YH-1898, FH-1046, YH-5427, FH-988, YH-5482, YH-5561, YH-5560, and YH-5568.
Purchase seed from registered dealers with receipts and keep empty seed bags.

**Sowing and Plant Density:**
Seed rate is 8 to 10 kg per acre with over 90 percent germination.
Sowing depth is 1.5 to 2 inches, and at least 2 inches in sandy soil.
Keep fields weed-free for the first 50 days.
Spring plant population per acre is 35,000 for hybrids and 26,000 to 30,000 for general varieties.
Kharif plant population per acre is 30,000 for hybrids and 23,000 to 26,000 for general varieties.

**Soil Fertility and Fertilizer per Acre:**
Poor soil with organic matter under 0.87 percent, phosphorus under 7 ppm, and potash under 80 ppm requires 119 kg nitrogen, 69 kg phosphorus, and 50 kg potash.
Medium soil with organic matter 0.87 to 1.29 percent, phosphorus 7 to 14 ppm, and potash 80 to 180 ppm requires 92 kg nitrogen, 58 kg phosphorus, and 37 kg potash.
Fertile soil with organic matter over 1.29 percent, phosphorus over 14 ppm, and potash over 180 ppm requires 75 kg nitrogen, 46 kg phosphorus, and 25 kg potash.

**Pest Control and Seed Treatment:**
Treat each kilogram of seed before sowing with Azoxystrobin + Clothianidin + Fludioxonil 72 percent at 9 grams, Imidacloprid + Tebuconazole 37.25 FS or 372.5 percent at 10 ml, Azoxystrobin + Clothianidin 62.5 percent WS at 9 grams, Thiamethoxam 350 FS at 10 ml, Thiamethoxam 70 WS at 3 grams, or Imidacloprid 70 WS at 5 grams.
This protects against diseases and shoot fly for 40 days.
If shoot fly attacks, spray Emamectin benzoate 1.9 EC at 200 ml or Bifenthrin 10 EC at 250 ml per acre at complete germination and again after 8 to 10 days.

**Disease and Field Management:**
Sow disease-resistant, heat-resistant varieties in spring and avoid mono-cropping.
Do not let crops face water stress during pollination, shorten irrigation intervals in heat, and drain excess rain.
To manage stem rot, cob rot, and smut, avoid weak-stemmed varieties, do not overuse nitrogen, ensure adequate potash, apply fungicide seed treatment, destroy infected crop residue, and rotate crops for several years.
aspects.weeds:
Emergence and Field Management:
Quality seed, soft and friable land preparation, and laser land leveling are required for uniform emergence and growth.
Maize seed depth must be 1.5 to 2 inches.
Keep the field free of weeds for the first 50 days.
Ensure effective pest control, uniform plant spacing, and uniform fertilizer broadcasting.
Never cultivate maize on sandy soil.
Keep fields moist in watter condition and do not let them dry out.
Destroy crop stubble and rotavate empty land.
Keep fields, water channels, and field ridges free of weeds year-round to prevent mite or louse attacks.
In case of mite attack, spray according to agricultural expert advice.

Weed Yield Impact and Mechanical Control:
Weeds can reduce maize yield by 30 to 50 percent in some cases.
Weed eradication is essential for full crop yield.
Hoeing can be done for weed control in small-scale maize cultivation.

Pre-Emergence Weed Control:
Apply Atrazine plus S-metolachlor 720 SC at 800 ml per acre for all types of weeds.
Apply this pre-emergence spray within 24 to 48 hours of sowing.

Post-Emergence Weed Control:
Apply Mesotrione plus Atrazine 48 SC at 650 ml per acre for dila, thick grass, and broadleaf weeds when all weeds have emerged.
If dila is not controlled, spray Mesotrione plus Atrazine 48 SC a second time at 650 ml per acre after an interval of 15 to 20 days.
Apply Halosulfuron-methyl 75 WDG at 20 grams per acre for dila after dila emerges.
Apply Atrnosafliopole 19.07 percent at 132 ml per acre for grass and broadleaf weeds from emergence up to the 3-leaf stage.

Spray Application Rules:
Use recommended poisons according to recommended methods.
Strictly avoid hoeing immediately after herbicide application.
Hoeing immediately after spray breaks the chemical effect and allows weeds to regrow.
Hoeing after spray raises dust that carries chemicals into the farmer body and breath, causing severe health harm.
